title: Norms
lead: Norms are the fourth of the seven ideas, and they cover the rules for how people are expected to behave.

p: Norms are social rules and expectations about how people should behave. They are learned through socialisation and can vary between cultures or change over time.
In plain words, norms are the unwritten rules for how to behave.

writers.name: Functionalists
writers.says: argue that shared norms make behaviour more predictable and help people cooperate.

list: Taking turns when speaking is a norm that parents and carers may teach, reinforced through praise.
Teaching greetings to children passes norms between generations, and what counts as a polite greeting may differ between cultural settings.
Queuing for a bus and good table manners are norms of general behaviour that children learn in the family.
Saying “please” is a norm that children learn when adults model the behaviour and praise the child.
Putting your phone away when a teacher or a friend is talking to you is a norm that many young people learn.
Using headphones instead of a speaker to watch videos on a bus is a norm that many people expect.

p: Define the term: Norms are social rules and expectations about how people should behave. They are learned through socialisation and can vary between cultures or change over time.
Item link: The parents and carers in the item may teach a child to take turns when speaking, reinforcing an everyday expectation through praise.
Explain with an example: Teaching greetings to children illustrates the transmission between generations in the item. What counts as a polite greeting may differ between cultural settings.
Theory link: Functionalists argue that shared norms make behaviour more predictable and help people cooperate.

quote.t: Culture varies between societies and is passed between generations through socialisation. Parents and carers are important in teaching children their earliest everyday expectations about behaviour.
